title: Longest Consecutive Sequence

theory_refs.at: "n ≤ 10⁵, must be O(n)" on unsorted input
theory_refs.why: The O(n) requirement is the hint that rules out sorting.

theory_refs.at: ↳ Bottleneck: a run of length L is walked L times
theory_refs.why: Why the naive set version is O(n²) and the start-of-run fix.

theory_refs.at: `for (int v : s)` — the set, not the array
theory_refs.why: Duplicates in the array would restart the same walk.

theory_refs.at: "each value is visited by at most one walk"
theory_refs.why: Why a loop inside a loop can still be O(n).

note:
1. Problem
   • Longest run of consecutive integers in an unsorted array, O(n) (LC 128)
2. Pattern: set + start of run
   • Trigger: "consecutive", unsorted, **O(n)** (rules out sorting)
3. Brute → optimal
   • Sort + scan → O(n log n) ✗
   • Set + walk from every value → O(n²) on 1..n
       ◦ Bottleneck: a run of length L is walked L times
   • Walk only from starts (v−1 missing) → O(n)
4. Pitfalls
   • Iterate the **set**, not the array (duplicates)
5. Remember
   • A loop inside a loop can be O(n) if each element is charged to one walk
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(unsorted array) → length of the longest set of values that form consecutive integers v, v+1, …, v+L−1 (positions do not matter).
- n ≤ 10⁵, must be O(n).
- [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2] → 4 (1, 2, 3, 4).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ This is a DISGUISE: nothing says "hash set", but the O(n) requirement on unsorted data does.
✍️ By hand: I look at 4 and ask "is 5 there? is 3 there?". If I always start counting from the smallest number of a run, I count each run once.
✍️ Hard part: avoiding counting the same run many times.
✍️ Edges: empty array → 0; duplicates [1, 2, 0, 1] → 3; negatives.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** For each value v, check v+1, v+2, … by scanning the array each time. O(n³) worst.
✍️ **2. Better.** Sort, then scan counting runs and skipping duplicates. O(n log n) — fails the O(n) requirement.
✍️ **3. Better.** Put values in a set; for each value walk upward with O(1) lookups. O(n²) on input like 1..n (each run walked from every element).
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: a run of length L is walked L times.
✍️ ↳ Unlock: every run has exactly one start — the value whose predecessor is missing. Walk only from starts.
✍️ **4. Optimal.** Set + start-of-run. Each value is part of exactly one walk → O(n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Insert all values into a hash set.
✍️ 2. For each value v in the set: if v − 1 is also in the set, skip it (not a start).
✍️ 3. Otherwise walk v+1, v+2, … while present, counting the length.
✍️ 4. Keep the maximum length.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   s = set(a); best = 0
LOOP    for v in s                       (the set, so duplicates are gone)
CHECK     if (v - 1) in s: continue      (not the start of a run)
UPDATE    len = 1
          while (v + len) in s: len++
          best = max(best, len)
RETURN  best
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) average time: n inserts; each value is checked once as a possible start and visited at most once by a walk. O(n) space.
>> detour cx-amortised-analysis#counting-trick | Why the inner while loop does not make this O(n²) | 3 min
✍️ Empty input → the loop never runs → 0.
- `v + len` with v near INT_MAX could overflow in theory; LeetCode's range is ±10⁹, so it is safe.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) required + unsorted + "consecutive / sequence" → hash set, not sorting.
✍️ To count each group once, start only from its canonical first member.
✍️ A loop inside a loop can still be O(n) if each element is charged to one inner walk.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Return the sequence itself.* Remember the start of the best run.
- *Streaming input?* Union-find or a map of run boundaries (value → length of run ending/starting here), updating neighbours on insert.
- *Why not sort?* O(n log n) violates the requirement; mention it as the simpler fallback.

siblings.title: Longest Square Streak in an Array
siblings.maps: "Next element" is v² instead of v+1; same set lookups, walking from each value.
siblings.note:
• Successor is v² instead of v+1 → set lookups again
• long long + stop above 10⁵ · answer −1 if < 2

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Longest subsequence that, after sorting, has each element equal to the square of the previous; length ≥ 2, else −1.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Put values in a set. From each v, walk v → v² → v⁴ while present. Values ≤ 10⁵ so a chain has at most ~5 steps → O(n · 5). (Start-of-run trick optional here because chains are tiny.)

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ For each value, follow squares through the set counting the chain; track the max; return −1 if < 2.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
s = set(a); best = 0
for v in s:
    len = 0; x = v
    while x in s: len++; x = x*x   (long long, stop if x > 1e5)
    best = max(best, len)
return best >= 2 ? best : -1
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body:
✍️ The "successor" can be any function (v+1, v², 2v); set membership makes each step O(1) ([[hash-set-runs#idea]]).
✍️ Squaring overflows int fast → `long long` and a bound check ([[cpp-integer-overflow#where]]).

siblings.title: Intersection of Two Arrays
siblings.maps: Set membership across two inputs; a second set removes duplicates from the answer.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Distinct values present in both arrays.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Set of the first array; for each value of the second that is in the set, output it once (erase it from the set after use).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Build a set from a; scan b; output and erase on a hit.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
s = set(a); out = []
for x in b: if x in s: out.append(x); s.erase(x)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ `erase(key)` returns how many were removed — a neat "was it there?" check.

siblings.title: First Missing Positive
siblings.maps: A set solves it in O(n) space; the O(1)-space version places each value v at index v−1 (cyclic placement).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Smallest positive integer not in the array; O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
✍️ The answer is in 1..n+1, so only values in [1, n] matter.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Set of values, then test 1, 2, 3, … → O(n) time, O(n) space. For O(1): swap each value v ∈ [1, n] into position v−1 until positions are stable; then the first i with a[i] ≠ i+1 gives i+1.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Cyclic placement, then scan for the first misplaced index.

stages.title: Pseudocode
Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body:
✍️ Each swap puts one value in its final place → O(n) total ([[arr-in-place-tricks#cyclic]]).
✍️ The guard `a[a[i]−1] != a[i]` stops infinite swapping on duplicates.
